# Vendor

`admin.obj.core.vendor` · v2.0.0 · **draft** · scope **core**

> An external party we buy from, pay, and are exposed to. A vendor record is three things at once and confusing them is how the function fails. It is a PAYMENT INSTRUCTION, and that is the part that gets attacked — a changed bank account on a plausible email is the cheapest large fraud in existence, and it succeeds because the change arrives through a channel we already trust. It is a DILIGENCE POSITION, and that decays silently: insurance lapses, a DPA goes unsigned, a screening result ages out, and nothing in the vendor master ever turns red on its own. And it is a DEPENDENCY, which nobody measures until the vendor fails, at which point substitutability — not price, not performance, not spend — is the only property that matters.


**The discriminator.** A vendor is a party we can PAY. The test is the payment instruction, not the relationship: a partner we exchange data with but never pay is a stakeholder; a counterparty on a signed agreement with live bank details in our ledger is a Vendor, however small the spend and however long since anyone spoke to them.


Also called: `Supplier`, `Counterparty`, `Third Party`, `Payee`, `Trade Creditor`, `Processor`


### Questions this object answers

- May this party be contracted with and paid today, and on whose authority?
- Have the bank details changed, who verified them, and by what channel?
- Is the diligence still true, or merely still on file?
- What stops if this vendor stops tomorrow, and how long would a replacement take?
- How much of this category's spend sits with this one party, across how many contracts?
- Has anybody looked at this relationship even once since the day it was onboarded?
- If we offboarded them this week, what would still be live — access, assets, mandates, data?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- NOT the paper. admin.obj.core.contract owns term, notice, obligations and the exit window; this object owns the party those obligations run against.
- NOT the bill. admin.obj.core.invoice owns the individual claim for payment and the three-way match.
- NOT the commitment of funds. admin.obj.core.budget_line owns whether the money exists.
- NOT the service targets. admin.obj.core.service_level owns the thresholds and the credits.
- NOT an employee, however long the contractor has been here. admin.obj.core.employee_record owns people we employ, and the boundary between the two is a tax and employment-status question, not an administrative preference.
- NOT the internal owner of the relationship — admin.obj.core.stakeholder is the person, this is the party.

## Preconditions

- **`vn.legal_identity_resolved`** The party is resolved to a legal entity and a registration number, not to a trading name in an email signature. _(unmet → Block creation of a payable record; degrade everything else. A vendor master keyed on name will acquire the duplicate whether or not anyone intended it, and the duplicate is permanent.
)_
- **`vn.diligence_tier_set_before_diligence_starts`** The diligence tier is decided from category and criticality BEFORE the checking begins. _(unmet → Default to standard and flag it. Proportionality decided in advance is a control; proportionality decided halfway through, while chasing a certificate somebody has refused to send, is a negotiation.
)_
- **`vn.payment_instruction_verified_before_first_payment`** The bank mandate has been verified out of band, by a named person, before any payment is released. _(unmet → Block payment. Not degrade. This is the one gate on this object that has no proportionate weaker version.)_
- **`vn.named_internal_owner`** A named internal owner exists before the vendor reaches active. _(unmet → Degrade — record the vendor, flag the gap, and route the review to the budget holder in the meantime. An unowned vendor is not an unusable one; it is an unreviewed one, and saying so is more useful than blocking.
)_
- **`vn.dpa_before_processing`** Where the vendor will process personal data, an executed DPA and an Article 30 entry exist before the first transfer. _(unmet → Block the data flow specifically, not the whole relationship. Blocking the commercial contract to force a DPA gets the DPA signed unread.)_
- **`vn.screening_current_at_admission`** Sanctions and adverse-media screening has been run within the tier's currency window, not merely at some point in the past. _(unmet → Block approval. Screening that is a year old is a statement about last year, and the lists change weekly.)_
- **`vn.category_spend_visible`** Total category spend is resolvable, so this vendor's share can be computed. _(unmet → Degrade to absolute spend and say so. Concentration expressed without a denominator is a number, not a risk position.)_


## Constraints

- **`vn.no_payment_to_unverified_account`** No payment may be released to a bank account whose fingerprint has changed since the last verification.
- **`vn.verification_must_be_out_of_band`** Verification must use a channel and a contact held BEFORE the change request arrived.
- **`vn.four_eyes_on_master_data`** A change to vendor bank details requires a second person, and it may not be the person who received the request.
- **`vn.segregation_of_duties`** The person who creates or amends a vendor record may not approve a payment to it.
- **`vn.no_payment_before_approved`** A vendor not in approved or active state cannot be paid.
- **`vn.no_processing_without_dpa`** Personal data may not flow to a data_processor vendor before an executed DPA exists.
- **`vn.critical_vendor_needs_exit_plan`** A vendor with criticality critical and substitutability none must hold a documented exit plan. _(soft)_


## Business rules

- **`vn.bank_change_requires_out_of_band_verification`** A change to bank_account_fingerprint must be verified by callback to a number held before the change request arrived, and recorded against a named verifier. Never a number contained in the request; never confirmed by reply.
 — _This single rule prevents more loss than every other control on this object combined._
- **`vn.bank_change_freezes_payment`** Payments are held from the moment a change is REQUESTED, not from the moment it is applied, until verification completes. — _The pressure to release "just this one, they are chasing" is itself part of the attack, and it is applied by the attacker in the attacker's own words._
- **`vn.no_payment_before_approved`** A vendor not in approved or active state cannot be paid.
- **`vn.data_processor_needs_dpa`** Where data_processor is true and dpa_signed is false, personal data must not flow.
- **`vn.duplicate_registration_number`** Two active vendor records sharing a registration_number must be merged before either is paid. — _Duplicates pay the same invoice twice and let a rejected supplier return under a variant spelling. Both failures are silent._
- **`vn.expired_diligence_blocks_new_work`** Expired diligence or lapsed insurance suspends new purchase orders. It does not suspend existing obligations. — _Conflating the two produces a control nobody will operate, because operating it would stop the building being cleaned._
- **`vn.never_reviewed_is_a_finding`** A critical vendor with never_reviewed true is an audit finding waiting to be written. Report it as one before the auditor does.
- **`vn.checklist_that_never_rejects`** An onboarding checklist that has produced no rejected state in twelve months is not running. It is being completed.
 — _A gate with a 100% pass rate is a form. Naming it as a control failure is the only way anyone will look at the criteria._
- **`vn.offboarding_is_four_steps_not_one`** A vendor cannot reach archived until access is revoked, the bank mandate is deactivated, assets are recovered and open purchase orders are closed.
 — _Offboarding is the step the process forgets, which is why dormant payable records outnumber active ones in most masters._
- **`vn.self_service_change_still_needs_verification`** A bank-detail change made through the supplier portal is subject to the same out-of-band verification as one requested by email. — _A portal changes who typed the digits. It does not change who was in control of the credentials, and it removes the human who might have paused._


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **Banks do genuinely merge and re-number accounts, so a legitimate change can arrive with a plausible institutional explanation.** — The exception is that the elevated change count is EXPLAINED. It is emphatically not that verification is waived — a bank migration is the single best cover story available to an attacker and it is used precisely because it is true often enough to be believable. Verify by callback anyway; record the explanation next to the verification.
 _(overrides vn.bank_details_change_requested)_
- **Where a vendor is the only possible supplier, a failed diligence item is a risk to be accepted at the right level rather than a gate that stops the relationship.** — Pretending a sole-source supplier can be rejected produces a fictional control and a real workaround. The honest mechanism is documented acceptance, named, dated, at a level proportionate to the exposure, with a review date — not a quiet exemption in a spreadsheet.
 _(overrides vn.expired_diligence_blocks_new_work, vn.no_payment_before_approved)_
- **A vendor may be admitted on abbreviated diligence for a genuine emergency, provided the admission carries a hard expiry.** — Emergencies are real and a process that cannot accommodate one is bypassed permanently rather than temporarily. The expiry is what keeps the exception an exception: without it the 2022 emergency supplier is still in the master in 2026, still payable, diligence never completed, and nobody can now say who admitted them.
 _(overrides vn.no_payment_before_approved, vn.data_processor_needs_dpa)_
- **A group company does not need third-party diligence, but it does need identity, a verified bank mandate and transfer-pricing terms.** — Applying the full third-party model to a sister company is theatre. Applying nothing is how an intercompany payment goes to an account nobody verified, on the reasoning that it is "internal" — the payment leaves the same building either way.
 _(overrides vn.expired_diligence_blocks_new_work)_
- **For utilities and regulated monopolies the terms are dictated and there is no meaningful diligence to run.** — There is no alternative supplier and no negotiation, so the checklist can only record. The correct posture is a minimal record and no pretence of a control, which also stops these vendors flattering the rejection-rate metric.
 _(overrides vn.checklist_that_never_rejects, vn.critical_vendor_needs_exit_plan)_
- **A supplier engaged through a public-sector or industry framework inherits the framework's vetting for admission purposes.** — Duplicating the framework's diligence wastes the capacity that should go to the unframeworked long tail. What is NOT inherited is currency — the framework vetted them on a date, and that date ages exactly like ours does.
 _(overrides vn.expired_diligence_blocks_new_work)_
- **Below a de minimis threshold, and with no data access and no site access, simplified diligence is proportionate.** — Enhanced diligence on a one-off £400 supplier is how a function loses credibility and gets routed around for everything else. The two conditions matter more than the threshold: spend is a poor proxy for risk, and a small supplier with system access is not a small risk.
 _(overrides vn.never_reviewed_is_a_finding)_
- **A vendor may be entirely healthy and silent — an annual licence renewed by direct debit generates no correspondence at all.** — Dormant is a flag for review, never for suspension. Suspending a silent supplier breaks a working relationship with a control and teaches the business to route around the master, which costs more than the risk the flag was raised for.
 _(overrides vn.dormant_but_still_payable)_


## Best practices

- **Verify every bank-detail change by calling a number held in the record BEFORE the request arrived, and record the named verifier.** — The whole attack depends on controlling every channel the verification could use. A number you already held is the one thing the attacker cannot have supplied. Four minutes of awkward phone call against a six-figure irrecoverable payment is the best trade in the administrative function.

- **Freeze payments automatically from the moment a change is REQUESTED, not from the moment it is applied.** — It removes the decision from the person under pressure. Between request and application is exactly the window the attacker is working in, and it is also the window in which somebody helpful applies the change to get ahead of the payment run.

- **Record when each diligence item STOPS being true, not when it was done.** — A completion date makes the master a history; an expiry date makes it a control. It is a one-column change and it is the difference between a supply base that is checked and one that was checked once, in 2021, by somebody who has left.

- **Set category and diligence tier first, then run the template for that tier.** — One universal checklist over-asks the cleaner and under-asks the processor. The cleaner's supplier stops replying and the processor sails through, which is precisely backwards, and everybody learns that diligence is paperwork rather than judgement.

- **Set the review interval from criticality and data access, never from spend.** — The most critical vendor in most organisations is a small one — the single-source integration between payroll and the bank. Sorting the review calendar by spend reviews the coffee supplier annually and that integration never.

- **Require a named internal owner as a condition of the vendor reaching active.** — Named on the day someone is enthusiastic about the supplier, it costs nothing. Named three years later it means whoever holds the budget code, who has no view on whether the relationship is any good.

- **For any processor, obtain and hold the subprocessor list, and treat additions as a change requiring review.** — Our exposure runs three tiers down whether or not we asked. Article 28 says we agreed to the list; in most organisations nobody in the building could produce it, which means we agreed to something we cannot describe.

- **Offboard against a fixed list — access revoked, mandate deactivated, assets recovered, purchase orders closed, records retained.** — Offboarding has no natural deadline and no complaining stakeholder, so it is done partially or not at all. A payable record with live access and an unreturned laptop is not an ended relationship, it is an unmonitored one.

- **For critical single-source vendors, price the alternative and time the switch before the renewal window opens.** — Substitutability written in a field without ever being tested is a guess. Tested, it is leverage — and it is the only leverage available against a supplier who knows perfectly well that we cannot leave.

- **Report onboarding rejections as a rate, by category, alongside the reasons.** — A checklist that has never rejected a vendor is not running, and nobody notices because nothing fails. The rate is the only signal that the gate closes, and publishing it is usually enough to make the criteria get read.



## Anti-patterns

- **Confirming a bank-detail change by replying to the address that requested it.** — tempting because It feels like verification — a second message, a written confirmation, a name at the bottom. It is fast, it is documented, and it produces an audit trail that looks exactly like a control operating correctly.
 Instead: Callback to a number held before the request arrived, by a named person, recorded against the record. Nothing else counts as verification.
- **Letting suppliers change their own bank details in a self-service portal with no human verification.** — tempting because It removes an administrative burden, it looks modern, and the supplier authenticated — so it feels stronger than an email, not weaker.
 Instead: Treat a portal change exactly like an emailed one: freeze payments, callback, second person to release.
- **An onboarding checklist that has produced no rejection in twelve months.** — tempting because Every item gets completed because completion is the measured outcome. Rejecting a supplier creates work, an argument with the business, and a delay somebody will be blamed for.
 Instead: Report the rejection rate by category with reasons. Convert never-rejecting items to recorded information and put the effort into the items that could fail.
- **Filing the insurance certificate and not recording the date it expires.** — tempting because The task was "obtain the certificate" and the certificate was obtained. The folder is complete and the tick is green.
 Instead: Make the expiry date the required field and the certificate the attachment, not the other way round.
- **Matching and deduplicating vendor records on name rather than on registration number.** — tempting because Names are what people type and what the invoice shows. Registration numbers require a lookup nobody built into the intake form.
 Instead: Require the registration number at intake, match on it, and block a second active record that shares one.
- **Sorting the vendor review calendar by spend.** — tempting because Spend is the one field that is always populated and always accurate. Criticality requires a judgement somebody has to own.
 Instead: Sort by criticality and data access. Populate criticality once at admission; it changes rarely and it is the field the whole programme should turn on.
- **Treating vendor management as an admission gate rather than a lifecycle.** — tempting because Onboarding has a requester, a deadline and somebody chasing it. Ongoing review has none of those three, and nothing bad visibly happens when it is skipped.
 Instead: Diarised reviews from criticality, and report never_reviewed_share as a headline number rather than a drill-down.
- **Ending the commercial relationship without deactivating the bank mandate, revoking access or recovering assets.** — tempting because The relationship ends when the work stops, and the work stopping is what everyone notices. Nobody is inconvenienced by a dormant payable record — the supplier is not chasing us and the business has moved on.
 Instead: Offboard against the five-point list and report offboarding completeness. Recovery fails silently because nobody is inconvenienced by an unreturned laptop except the balance sheet.
- **A performance scorecard on which no vendor has ever scored badly.** — tempting because The scores are set by the relationship owner, who negotiated the contract, chose the supplier, and will have to sit in the review meeting. A low score is a conversation nobody wants and a criticism of their own decision.
 Instead: Score against dated SLA evidence rather than opinion, and track credits_claimed separately. If nothing has ever been claimed, nothing is being measured.
- **Releasing a payment outside the process because the supplier is chasing and the business says it is urgent.** — tempting because The urgency is real, the supplier is known, and the person refusing looks like an obstacle. The exception is granted once, by somebody senior, with the best of intentions.
 Instead: Keep the freeze and shorten the verification instead — the callback takes four minutes. Speed the control, never the exception.

## Inputs

- **email** — onboarding correspondence, who is waiting on whom
- **email** — which side is holding the onboarding pack
- **derived** — responsiveness trajectory during onboarding
- **erp** — vendor master, bank details, spend, payment history
- **register** — companies registry — legal name, status, directors, filings
- **regulator** — sanctions and PEP lists, licence registers, debarment lists
- **document** — insurance certificates, filed accounts, policies, the DPA
- **signed_form** — executed vendor form and bank mandate on their letterhead
- **phone** — callback verification to a number held before the request arrived
- **attestation** — self-declarations — modern slavery, conflicts, security posture
- **portal** — supplier self-service submissions
- **access_log** — third-party account activity and last use


## Outputs

- **`payment_integrity_flag`** Bank details changed, unverified, or verified by a method that does not count. Must reach a named human the same day. → L4.decision_maker, L5.execution_planning
- **`verification_channel`** How this counterparty must be contacted to verify a payment change — a held number, never a number contained in the request. The one place the channel IS the control. → L5.2.channel_planner
- **`vendor_readiness`** Whether this party may be contracted with and paid today. → L4.decision_maker
- **`diligence_status`** Current, expiring or expired — naming the specific item, never a composite score. A red item must not be able to hide behind four green ones. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`dependency_profile`** What breaks if they stop, and for how long. The input a renewal negotiation is actually decided on. → L4.reasoning_unit, L5.communication_planning
- **`concentration_exposure_bp`** Share of category spend held by this counterparty, rolled up to the group parent. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`review_due_flag`** Interval elapsed, or never reviewed at all. The second is a different and worse finding than the first. → L5.execution_planning
- **`offboarding_residue`** What is still live after offboarding — access, assets, mandates, open purchase orders. → L4.reasoning_unit, L5.execution_planning


## Events

- **`vn.identified`** Counterparty Identified
- **`vn.diligence_started`** Diligence Started
- **`vn.bank_details_change_requested`** Bank Details Change Requested — invalidates bank_account_fingerprint, bank_details_verified_at, bank_details_verified_by, bank_verification_method
- **`vn.bank_details_verified`** Bank Details Verified
- **`vn.approved`** Vendor Approved
- **`vn.rejected`** Vendor Rejected
- **`vn.diligence_expired`** Diligence Expired — invalidates diligence_current, sanctions_screen_result
- **`vn.performance_breach`** Service Level Breached
- **`vn.went_quiet`** Counterparty Went Quiet
- **`vn.entity_changed`** Vendor Entity Changed By Acquisition Or Re-registration — invalidates sanctions_screen_result, diligence_current, bank_account_fingerprint, spend_share_bp
- **`vn.offboarded`** Vendor Offboarded


## Actions

- **Verify bank details by callback** (human) — To a number held before the request arrived. This single act prevents more loss than every other control on this object combined, and it takes four minutes.
- **Freeze payments pending verification** (system) — The default posture on any change to the payment instruction. Reversing it requires a second person who did not receive the request.
- **Escalate suspected payment fraud** (human) — Out of the administrative track immediately, to the bank and to the payment provider. Speed beats certainty here — the money is recoverable for hours, not days, and an apology for a false alarm is cheap.
- **Run the diligence pack** (human) — To the template for their category and tier, not the universal one. A universal checklist over-asks the cleaner and under-asks the processor, and teaches everyone that it is paperwork.
- **Screen against sanctions and adverse media** (system) — On admission and on the tier's interval. Annual screening against weekly lists is a control with a fifty-one-week blind spot.
- **Chase the outstanding onboarding item** (agent) —
- **Unblock the internal onboarding step** (agent) — Named internal owner, not the procurement mailbox. Most onboarding delay is ours and almost none of it is attributed to us.
- **Request renewed insurance and certificates** (agent) — Ahead of expiry. Requested after expiry it is a gap on the record whatever date the certificate eventually carries.
- **Schedule the periodic review** (system) — Interval set from criticality, not spend. The most critical vendor in most organisations is a small one.
- **Conduct the relationship review** (human) — Performance, diligence currency, concentration, price, and whether we would choose them again today. The last question is the one that produces the useful answer.
- **Rehearse the exit for a single-source dependency** (human) — Price the alternative and time the switch, before the renewal rather than during an outage. Without it, substitutability is a guess written in a field.
- **Offboard the vendor** (human) — Revoke access, deactivate the bank mandate, recover assets, close open purchase orders, retain the records. All five, or it is not offboarding. A dormant payable record is a live one.


## Evidence

- **register** · 9500 bp — Companies registry. Independent, dated and hard to forge — the strongest identity evidence available, and free.
- **regulator** · 9500 bp — Sanctions, debarment and licence registers. Authoritative and, for screening, dispositive. Decays fastest of anything here: lists change weekly.
- **phone** · 9000 bp — Callback to a previously held number. The strongest possible evidence that a payment instruction is genuine, and the control most often skipped for being slow.
- **contract** · 9000 bp — Executed agreement with the counterparty. Proves what was agreed, not who should be paid.
- **signed_form** · 8500 bp — Signed bank mandate or vendor form on their letterhead. Strong, and forgeable — which is why it corroborates a callback rather than replacing one.
- **erp** · 8000 bp — Vendor master and payment history. Authoritative for what we did, never for whether it was right.
- **access_log** · 8000 bp — Third-party account activity. The only source that shows a vendor relationship is still live after everyone believes it ended.
- **document** · 7000 bp — Insurance certificates and filed accounts. Check the expiry date, not the presence of the file.
- **attestation** · 6000 bp — Their signed self-declaration — modern slavery, conflicts, security posture. A statement of intent, not a verified fact, and it should never be scored as one.
- **portal** · 5000 bp — Supplier self-service submissions. Convenient, unverified, and the route by which bank details are changed with no human in the loop at all.
- **derived** · 3000 bp — Inferred from engagement shape. Corroborating only.
- **email** · 2000 bp — Correspondence claiming a change of details. Worth almost nothing and treated by most organisations as though it were worth everything. Scored deliberately low so that no pattern can reach a payment decision on it alone.


## Metrics

- **bank_change_verification_rate** (percent) — Share of bank-detail changes verified out of band, by callback, before the next payment run. The one metric on this object worth putting in front of a board.
- **mean_time_to_verify_bank_change** (hours) — Request to verified. The window in which the payment hold is doing all the work, and the window in which the business is pushing hardest to release it.
- **diligence_currency_rate** (percent) — Share of active vendors whose diligence has not expired. Distinct from the share who have ever been diligenced, which is the number usually reported.
- **never_reviewed_share** (percent) — Active vendors with no review since onboarding. Usually the most uncomfortable number in the pack and the easiest one to produce.
- **rejection_rate** (percent) — Share of onboarding attempts rejected. A rate of zero is not a clean supply base; it is a gate that does not close. A rate above about a fifth suggests the tiering is wrong rather than the suppliers.
- **onboarding_cycle_time** (days) — Request to approved, split by ball_in_court so the internal share is visible rather than assumed. The split is usually the reverse of the story the business tells.
- **unapproved_spend_share** (percent) — Payments made to vendors that never reached approved state.
- **category_concentration** (percent) — Largest vendor group's share of category spend. Group, not entity.
- **offboarding_completeness** (percent) — Share of offboarded vendors with access revoked, mandate deactivated, assets recovered and purchase orders closed. Usually far lower than anyone expects.
- **duplicate_master_records** (count) — Active records sharing a registration number.

## Examples

- **Long-standing supplier emails new bank details from a lookalike domain** _(typical)_ — Real thread, real signature block, plausible reason, urgent invoice attached, and a phone number in the footer. The only control that stops it is a call to a number nobody looked up in the email.
- **Cleaning contractor, insurance lapsed eighteen months ago** _(typical)_ — Still on site, still invoicing, still green in the master — because the master holds the certificate and not its expiry.
- **Single-source SaaS holding the payroll-to-bank integration** _(edge)_ — Low spend, criticality systemically_critical, substitutability none. Reviewed less often than the office coffee supplier, and the only vendor on the list that could stop payroll.
- **Vendor onboarded as an exception for an urgent project in 2022** _(edge)_ — Diligence never completed, record never closed, still payable in 2026. This is what onboarding_stalled turns into when nobody sets an expiry on the exception.
- **Same supplier under two records, 'Ltd' and 'Limited'** _(misclassification)_ — Two remittances, one genuine, one duplicate. Found by registration number and by nothing else — least of all by the eye of whoever approved both.
- **Processor with undisclosed subprocessors** _(edge)_ — Our data sits three tiers down with a party we have never named. Article 28 says we agreed to this; nobody in the building could list them.
- **Supplier acquired by a competitor; bank details change legitimately** _(edge)_ — Diligence is void, concentration has moved, and the one genuine reason for a bank change has arrived. Verify by callback anyway — this is the story an attacker would have chosen.
- **Marketing agency we stopped using in 2023, record still active and payable** _(misclassification)_ — Read as harmless dormancy. It is a live payment destination on an unwatched account, and a single plausible invoice against it would clear.
- **Contractor invoicing monthly through a personal service company for four years** _(misclassification)_ — Held as a vendor. It is an employment-status question with a tax consequence, and admin.obj.core.employee_record is where the answer lives.
- **Records-storage provider holding forty boxes of signed contracts** _(edge)_ — custodian_of, not merely a supplier. Offboard them without recovering the boxes and the executed counterparts are gone with the relationship.
- **Framework supplier vetted in 2021, engaged in 2026** _(counterexample)_ — The framework's vetting is inherited; its currency is not. A five-year-old screen against weekly-updated lists is not a screen.

## Metadata

owner **Admin** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> Rewritten onto the 23-section schema. Five of fourteen patterns are executable, and all five sit on the onboarding correspondence rather than on the vendor: contract_requested, legal_review, thread.ball_in_court, thread.last_inbound, derived.engagement and edge_count. The pipeline can see us negotiating with a counterparty and can see nothing at all about the counterparty.
Two backlog lines are worth funding before anything else in the Admin brain. First, bank_details_change_requested (L2) — the fraud arrives by email, on a real thread, in a mailbox Layer 2 already reads and is simply not looking at; it is the cheapest high-value extractor available. Second, vendor.bank_account_fingerprint (L1) — without it the change itself is invisible and only the payment is observable, which is the wrong half. Together they convert the highest-risk moment in the administrative function from an event found at reconciliation into an event caught before the payment run.
Two structural fixes follow closely. vendor.diligence_expires_at (L1) is a one-column change that turns a record of a control into a control: most masters store when a check was done and never when it stops being true. vendor.last_reviewed_at (L1) makes the ABSENCE of a review visible, which is the finding that matters — a vendor nobody has examined since onboarding is not low-risk, it is unmeasured, and today those two render identically in every report.
